summary:
Ingushetia is a republic of Russia and stands under the Russian national framework; the findings below concern conditions specific to the republic and the North Caucasus region.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) treats the North Caucasus, including Ingushetia, as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory assessment of Russia. It finds that trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, documents systematic regional campaigns against LGBT+ people between 2017 and 2024, and states that the 2023 extremist designation exposes LGBT+ activity to two to six years' imprisonment, rising to six to ten years for organising, with violence spreading beyond the region.

David Isteev of North Caucasus SOS, interviewed by the Human Rights House Foundation, states that there is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus and that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families. He attests that conditions in the region have deteriorated year on year; the interview carries no date in this record.

Global Affairs Canada advises avoid all travel to Russia and names Ingushetia among the republics with frequent terrorist attacks, alongside Chechnya, Dagestan and Stavropol Krai. The advisory records surveillance of foreigners and states that 2SLGBTQI+ persons, their allies and their families have been attacked, harassed and abused. It notes that since January 2024 organisations advocating for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as extremist, and that the Ministry of Interior requires special permission to enter certain areas.
tangentialFactors:
The UK Home Office finding places Ingushetia and the wider North Caucasus outside the otherwise non-persecutory assessment it makes of Russia as a whole, so conditions attributed to the republic are more severe than the national baseline in the same assessment.

The Canadian advisory's terrorist-attack designation for Ingushetia is a general security classification applied alongside its LGBT-specific warnings; it does not itself describe differential treatment of trans travellers, but it accompanies documented attacks on 2SLGBTQI+ persons and their families in the country.

The North Caucasus SOS testimony is a regional practitioner assessment without a stated date, and its claim of year-on-year deterioration is not attached to a specific period or count in this record.
localsOnly:
LGBTIQ+ residents of the North Caucasus, including Ingushetia, face violence, detention and forced return to families arising from private existence, according to North Caucasus SOS.

The UK Home Office documents systematic regional campaigns against LGBT+ people in the North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024, with activity exposed to two to six years' imprisonment under extremism provisions and six to ten years for organising.

Residents advocating publicly for 2SLGBTQI+ issues are treated as extremist by the authorities since January 2024, and entering certain areas of the republic requires special permission from the Ministry of Interior.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Ingushetia-specific incident log, homicide figure, or count of violence against trans residents appears in this inventory; the regional evidence consists of the UK Home Office assessment, the North Caucasus SOS testimony and the Canadian travel advisory, and no trans-specific killing rate for the republic is sourced.

The date of the Human Rights House Foundation interview with David Isteev is not given in this record, so the timing of the deterioration he describes cannot be fixed.

Region-level public-attitude survey data for Ingushetia is not sourced here; national polling figures sit with the parent record.

The detailed enforcement history of the extremist designation, including club raids, symbol-display arrests and the March to May 2026 outlawing of nine organisations, is national in scope and belongs to the parent record rather than to this republic.
